item.title: Internet traffic and attacks during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections
item.description: On November 3, 2026 U.S. voters headed to the polls. Here’s what Cloudflare data across more than 1,400 protected sites tells us about Election Day Internet traffic and cyberattacks.
item.dc:creator: Patrick Day
Jocelyn Woolbright
Carlos Azevedo
item.content:encoded:
Visitors to government election websites surged 363% on November 3, the date of the 2026 midterm elections in the United States. Across Cloudflare's election protection programs, we also detected a significant shift in the types and timing of cyberattacks throughout 2026.

Unlike what we saw in other recent elections, attackers focused on gaining access to internal systems and data, rather than knocking websites offline. Government election websites faced website vulnerability attempts 180 times more often than denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, and at roughly ten times the rate of Cloudflare's broader customer base. We also found evidence of at least one attempt to exploit a recently disclosed critical PHP vulnerability on a state government voting website in the Western United States.

These attacks peaked in late October, several weeks before the election. Vulnerability exploit attempts climbed steadily throughout 2026: from 200,000 per day in January, to 2 million per day in October. However, on Election Day in the U.S., Cloudflare detected no escalation in attack volume and zero major DDoS incidents across protected election sites, marking a sharp contrast to other recent elections, such as in Moldova last year.

Our data regarding cyberattacks on election institutions came from organizations participating in Cloudflare's free cybersecurity programs: the Athenian Project, Cloudflare for Campaigns, and Project Galileo. Together, these initiatives helped protect more than 1,400 election-related websites during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, including those belonging to state and local governments, candidates, political parties, voting-rights advocates, journalists, and civil society groups.

Cloudflare launched its first election protection program in 2016 after widespread reports of cyberattacks targeting the U.S. elections. A decade later, it is remarkable to see how far governments and campaigns have come in securing their digital infrastructure. We are proud to help protect democratic institutions and are encouraged that cyberattacks were once again not a disruptive factor in 2026.

In this post, we examine traffic and attacks observed against those organizations on Election Day, analyze the most common types of attacks of the 2026 cycle, and provide recommendations based on those findings.

Election Day: significant voter traffic, minimal attacks

Ordinary user traffic to state and local government election websites was higher on Election Day (November 3) than any other day in 2026. Traffic to those sites increased to approximately 602 million requests, up from 130 million on November 1. By comparison, traffic across the rest of Cloudflare’s global network rose by only 12% over the same period.

State and local government election websites provide authoritative information to voters on how to register, where to vote, and who won. Because of their critical role, these platforms are often targeted by those seeking to suppress voter turnout, disrupt the reporting of results, or steal sensitive information.

On Election Day itself, Cloudflare did not record a single significant distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack across any of its 1,400 election-related websites. The only significant DDoS attack occurred on November 2, targeting a candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives in California and totaled 520,000 requests. By comparison, the Moldovan Election Commission experienced more than 898 million malicious requests in a single 12-hour period on their Election Day in 2025, with attacks peaking at 324,333 requests per second.

Prior to Election Day: the most common attacks in the 2026 cycle

Website vulnerability scans were by far the most common attack observed by Cloudflare in the 2026 U.S. election cycle. In the 12 months leading up to the election, Cloudflare mitigated 392 million such attacks on government election websites alone.

Website vulnerability attacks exploit outdated or vulnerable website code to gain access to internal systems and data. For example, cross-site scripting attacks inject malicious code into web pages in order to capture administrator credentials or deface site content. SQL injection manipulates database queries allowing attackers to potentially extract voter records or alter data.

Phishing and other malicious emails targeting political campaigns protected by the company occurred at rates consistent with Cloudflare's broader network, but showed signs of sophistication. In the 90 days leading up to the election, 3.9% of emails sent to organizations participating in Cloudflare for Campaigns were identified as malicious, closely tracking the 4.8 percent baseline across other Cloudflare customers. However, nearly 42% of those malicious emails managed to bypass basic email authentication checks, such as verifying sender identity or preventing in-transit tampering. These threats were nonetheless identified by Cloudflare’s advanced phishing detection tools.

Although website vulnerabilities were the most common attack overall, for journalism and election-related civil society organizations, DDoS was the most common. Over the same 12-month period, Cloudflare mitigated over 10.8 billion DDoS requests targeting these groups. The largest single attack occurred on September 10, 2026, hitting a U.S.-based news organization with 3.04 billion requests. This pattern is consistent with Cloudflare research released earlier this year, which found that among all Project Galileo entities in 120 countries, DDoS were by far the most common attack seen, accounting for 81% of all attacks.

PHP vulnerability

On October 21, security researchers disclosed serious vulnerabilities (known as php2shell) in PHP, an open source back-end programming language used by 70% of the world's websites. The flaws reportedly could allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Cloudflare deployed Web Application Firewall (WAF) protections for all customers, prior to public disclosure of the vulnerability.

On October 22, Cloudflare's PHP defense was triggered more than 9,000 times on a state government election website in the Western U.S. This attack was only detected on one election-related site and appears to have been an isolated incident rather than part of a broader trend.

Recommendations

Cloudflare research consistently shows that individuals and organizations participating in democratic elections face significant risk of cyberattack. Data gathered during the 2026 U.S. midterm election suggests those attacks continue to evolve, occur throughout an election cycle and not only on Election Day, and can vary depending on the type of organization targeted.

Based on the recent cyberattack trends in the 2026 U.S. midterms and other elections, we make the following recommendations:  

  • Prepare for surges in user traffic. Legitimate voter interest can create traffic spikes that overwhelm unprepared infrastructure and make essential election websites inaccessible. Organizations should prepare scalable, efficient infrastructure to handle Election Day traffic increases without straining budgets or staff.  
  • Maintain security protections year-round, not just on Election Day. Cyberattacks targeting democratic institutions occur across the entire election cycle, not just around voting windows. Defensive postures must remain active continuously rather than treated as a short-term, seasonal measure.
  • Deploy automated defenses to counter rapid threats. AI has made it easier for attackers to find and exploit new vulnerabilities. Organizations should implement security services that update automatically, like managed rules, to ensure new protections deploy by default.

Ensuring voters have access to reliable information about elections not only helps encourage participation and deliver timely, accurate results, but also protects voter confidence in the democratic process itself. As more officials, more institutions, and the public increasingly rely on the Internet for those services, keeping that digital infrastructure stable, secure, and accessible becomes an essential civic priority.

State and local election offices, political campaigns, party organizations, journalists, and voting rights groups in need of cybersecurity services can access them from Cloudflare at no cost. Visit the Athenian Project (for state and local election websites), Cloudflare for Campaigns (for political campaigns), or Project Galileo (for civil society, democracy, and journalism organizations) to learn more about eligibility and sign up today.

item.title: An updated Clairic and Clairic-flash are now open-weight, from the new Workers AI Superintelligence team
item.description: Clairic graduates from preview, while Clairic-flash joins the repertoire on Workers AI. We’re doing an open-weight release for both extraction models.
item.dc:creator: Alex Reneau
Michelle Chen
Kevin Flansburg
item.content:encoded:
Cloudflare has become a neolab. We’re building our own frontier AI models for our customers and the open-source community.

Today, we’re announcing two open-weight model releases:

  • We’re introducing an updated version of Clairic. Since the preview, we’ve improved extraction from complex documents including images and PDFs (new!), with more reliable handling of tables, lists, and dates, and better grounding of answers in the source material.
  • We’re introducing Clairic-flash, a lighter, faster version of Clairic that delivers strong extraction and prediction performance in a compact, 9-billion-parameter model.

Both extraction models are hosted on Workers AI and full open weights are available on Hugging Face.

We’re also excited to re-introduce ourselves as the Workers AI superintelligence team, the frontier AI research team behind Clef, Clairic, and lots more in the works. This team is working quickly to push the AI frontier and build useful models for Cloudflare’s customers and the open source community.

A new version of Clairic: redesigned after the preview release

Since announcing Clairic in preview, we have received a ton of use cases and helpful feedback on how customers wanted to use an extraction model. We heard about use cases ranging from extracting data from images like receipts to reading values from support tickets. We knew that we wanted extraction to be the clear focus for the model, so it had to excel at reading from unstructured data.

We decided to go back to the drawing board with Clairic and redesigned our architecture, differentiating this new version of Clairic from our preview release. For ordinary text and number extraction fields, we now use parallel slot autoregressive generation instead of a single forward pass. Each field uses the tokens it has already written to choose its next token, then stops at its own end marker. All the fields advance together in the serving batch, still giving lightning-fast latency per request. This boosted our accuracy in extraction for both text and images, and the trade-off in accuracy offsets the small latency cost. For computation, estimation, and extraction use cases, we trained special heads that can handle estimates, forecasts, durations, calculated dates, and explicit arithmetic.

Although the model architecture evolved, we kept the parts of the typed API interface that make the answers useful: confidence scores, character spans, and probabilities are still intact with every request. The model is still incredibly fast and cheap. From the evals below, you can see how our newer versions of Clairic have greatly improved on extraction across text, images, PDFs, and more.

Our Clairic models excel across extraction use cases, but take these evals as directional guidance since they are self-reported. We wanted to show an illustrative picture of how Clairic is performing across generalized extraction use cases and celebrate the fact that other companies are releasing extraction models as well — confirming our original hypothesis that extraction was a pain point for LLM users because of the cost, latency, and accuracy.

But is it fast?

Better extraction for images and PDFs

In our preview blog post, Clairic read a photo of a receipt. Now the Clairic family of models can read PDFs too, so you can ask for the supplier, line items, and total in one request, even when they appear on different pages. You can include up to four images or PDF pages in total, and line items can come back as rows that keep each description, quantity, and price together. Due to Clairic’s new architecture, image reading accuracy has improved from 207 errors to 0 on our internal benchmarks, explicitly covering text and images.

Promotional pricing on Clairic for a limited time

When we first launched our preview endpoint of Clairic at @cf/cloudflare/clairic, we hosted the 9B variant as it was faster and easier to train, at the preview price of $0.10 per M input tokens. We’re now moving the 9B model to the @cf/cloudflare/clairic-flash endpoint and the 27B model will live at @cf/cloudflare/clairic.

The 27B Clairic model will be priced at $0.24 per M input tokens, while the 9B Clairic-flash model will be priced at $0.10 per M input tokens. Although the model does technically generate output tokens, we decided to keep the System One pricing principles and are only charging on input tokens: we eat the cost of the output token generation.

In order to make this a seamless swap, we’re offering a promotional discount on Clairic — until December 1, 2026, both Clairic and Clairic-flash will cost $0.10 per M input tokens. This means you get to try out the higher quality variant of Clairic at the same price. If your applications are hooked up to the Clairic endpoint that we released in preview, you will automatically benefit from the better extraction capabilities of our new model, which we’re rolling out in place.

If you’d like to move more cost-sensitive workloads to the cheaper 9B Clairic-flash variant, we encourage you to do so. On December 1, we’ll be ending the promotional discount for Clairic and pricing will resume at $0.24 per M input tokens instead of the discounted $0.10 per M input tokens.

Clairic and Clairic-flash (new) are open-weight

Both Clairic models are now open-weight on Hugging Face as well. We have seen an outpouring of experiments and tuned models from our release of Clef, and we’re happy to continue supporting teams and research with our open-weight release of Clairic.

Our mission with these System One models is to help people augment their expensive LLM usage with smaller, faster, cheaper models that are purpose-built for a specific task. We hope that releasing these models open-weight encourages others to experiment and build on our ideas as well.

Try them out

Clairic and Clairic-flash are available on Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clairic and @cf/cloudflare/clairic-flash. The developer documentation has the full API schemas, which remain unchanged from our preview endpoint. We’re also publishing the open-weight releases for Clairic and Clairic-flash on Hugging Face. 

The team behind these models — the Workers AI superintelligence team — is just getting started, and growing fast to push frontier AI research at Cloudflare. Join us early and help shape what the superintelligence team becomes.

item.title: How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)
item.description: Java4Shell is a critical memory-corruption flaw in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder that can lead to remote code execution. Cloudflare has released six WAF managed rules for paid plans that logs matching requests by default. Patch your Java runtimes now.
item.dc:creator: Denzil Correa
Daniele Molteni
Georgie Yoxall
Kuber Nandwani
item.content:encoded:
On November 17, 2026, the security research company Calif disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption vulnerability in the Base64 decoder of OpenJDK, the most widely used Java runtime. Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, it scores 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The flaw affects Java. OpenJDK published a security advisory and Oracle released patched builds in its November 2026 Critical Patch Update the same day, at 21:00 UTC.

The vulnerability lets a remote attacker with no credentials send malformed Base64 data to a Java application and overwrite memory next to the decoded output. Calif turned that overwrite into a leak of heap memory, similar to Heartbleed, and into remote code execution. Calif demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution against Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate in their default configurations, and post-authentication remote code execution against Apache Kafka, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker.

Cloudflare has released a new set of rules in the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset designed to detect malformed Base64 input patterns associated with this vulnerability. The rules are available on Pro, Business and Enterprise plans and are enabled by default with the Log action because malformed input and some benign application-specific token formats can resemble exploitation attempts. Blocking by default could therefore disrupt legitimate traffic. Customers can review matching requests in Security Events now and change the rules action to Block once they confirm it does not affect legitimate traffic. 

The WAF is an additional layer of defense, not a replacement for the patch. Java4Shell can be reached through paths a WAF does not see, like outbound TLS responses, and the only complete fix is to update the Java runtime. Our analysts continue to monitor attack activity and will update the rules as new techniques and variations appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and get more information on how the vulnerability develops on the dedicated Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing.

We have seen no indication so far that Java4Shell was exploited on Cloudflare infrastructure.

What we know about the vulnerability

Base64 is a common way to represent binary data as text. Java applications decode Base64 when they process authentication headers, tokens, file uploads and many network messages. To decode it faster, OpenJDK replaces frequently used code with specialized machine code, called intrinsics. On supported x86-64 processors, the Base64 intrinsic uses AVX-512 instructions to process 64 bytes at a time.

The bug sits in the handwritten assembly that handles the final characters of the input. When the tail of the input contains padding characters (=) in a position where valid Base64 never places them, the routine calculates a negative output length. That invalid length turns into a full 64-byte write. For a 65-character input, made of 64 characters followed by a single =, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte output array and then writes 62 bytes past its end.

Java eventually rejects the input as invalid and throws an exception. By then, the neighboring memory has already been overwritten. An application's own input validation does not help, because the corruption happens inside the decoder before the application can reject the data.

The simplest trigger is 64 A characters followed by =. On OpenJDK 17, the trigger needs 128 characters followed by =, because the threshold for the fast code path is higher.

Exploitation is not point-and-shoot. The overwritten bytes are mostly fixed values, and the attacker controls only where the write lands. To build a working exploit, Calif arranged the Java heap so that the overflow enlarged neighboring arrays, which gave them first a way to read heap memory and then a way to write chosen bytes. Each target application requires its own exploit chain. Calif reported developing its first working local exploit in about three hours with the help of AI agents, so we expect other attackers to build exploit chains quickly.

Who is affected

Java4Shell affects a system only when all the following conditions are true:

Condition

Details

Java runtime

OpenJDK 17.0.6 or newer, including distributions built from OpenJDK: Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, Red Hat OpenJDK, Oracle OpenJDK, Oracle Java SE and Oracle GraalVM for JDK.

Check Oracle's advisory for the exact list of affected Oracle builds.

Processor

x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI support, such as Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids and Granite Rapids, or AMD EPYC and Ryzen Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 processors are not affected.

Input

The application decodes attacker-controlled Base64 data with the standard Java decoder.

Many applications bundle their own Java runtime, and container images ship with a fixed Java Development Kit (JDK). Upgrading the system Java package does not update those copies, and it does not replace a Java virtual machine (JVM) that is already running. Every updated service needs a restart.

Mitigate if you cannot patch right away

If you cannot update immediately, Calif documents two JVM startup flags that remove the vulnerable code path:

  • -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics disables hardware-accelerated Base64 encoding and decoding.
  • -XX:UseAVX=2 disables AVX-512. Apply this flag only on x86-64 hosts. OpenJDK on ARM does not recognize it and will fail to start.

Both flags require a restart and may reduce performance for workloads that decode large amounts of Base64. They buy time while you patch. They do not replace the update.

Protect your infrastructure while you patch

Patching every Java runtime takes time, especially when JDKs are bundled inside applications and container images. Cloudflare WAF can reduce your exposure while you patch. A new managed rule, available on paid plans and enabled in Log mode by default, detects the malformed Base64 input that triggers Java4Shell. For Business and Enterprise customers, WAF attack score adds a machine learning layer that scores each request for remote code execution payloads, which helps catch variations and bypass attempts that signature-based rules can miss.

New managed rules

Protection for paid plans has been released as part of the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Ruleset ID efb7b8c949ac4650a09736fc376e9aee). The rule is enabled by default with the Log action, because blocking by default could cause false positives on legitimate Base64 traffic. To review its matches, go to Security > Security Analytics > Events and filter by the rule ID. If the matches are not legitimate traffic, change the rule action to Block: go to Security > Settings, edit the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, search for CVE-2026-114938 and set the rule action to Block. Alternatively, you can follow the link to review your configuration on the Zero Wire briefing.

Rule description

Rule ID

Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 Header - CVE-2026-114938

5de9b20a45ea45d3841919ab4d718bf4

Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 Query Value - CVE-2026-114938

46bb4172813e471ea62d31c02337b51d

Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 Body Value - CVE-2026-114938

d4dc3f71f1bc44a0811ae570e5e5836c

Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 Path Segment - CVE-2026-114938

0dceaf0684b54fd0b085fcfb6fd6f152

Java4Shell - Malformed Base64url JWT Component - CVE-2026-114938

0ddd0eb664a040779f2f19065a25d991

Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 WebAuthn Value - CVE-2026-114938

4fce1ea79a614c07a27348d167d74ebb

We are working on a rule for the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and will update this post when it is available.

A WAF can block the exploit when the malformed Base64 arrives in an HTTP request that passes through Cloudflare. It cannot block every path to the vulnerable decoder, including:

  • Encoded or nested data. The Base64 value may be wrapped inside another encoding or compressed format that the application unpacks before decoding.
  • Non-HTTP protocols. Some affected products, such as the Apache Kafka broker, accept traffic over their own protocols.
  • Outbound connections. Calif also shared a client-side exploit: a Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own.
  • Traffic that bypasses Cloudflare. This includes internal traffic between services.

Adding defense-in-depth with WAF attack score

While the managed rule is the primary way to block malformed Base64 triggers at the edge, Cloudflare WAF Attack Score (and specifically its remote code execution sub-score cf.waf.score.rce available on Enterprise plans) can offer an additional, complementary layer of protection.

Because CVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell) is a binary heap-corruption vulnerability, an attacker rarely achieves full, reliable remote code execution with a single 65-byte (or 129-byte) trigger string alone. On the wire, that initial trigger looks like an opaque, malformed Base64 string containing heap-corruption bytes rather than traditional web-layer injection syntax. As a result, machine learning models trained on application-layer injection patterns will not flag the raw Base64 trigger in isolation.

Instead, turning a bounded JVM heap overflow into remote code execution over HTTP almost always requires a multi-stage or multi-parameter exploit chain, which creates more fingerprints that WAF Attack Score can inspect and flag, including:

  • Heap Grooming and Triggering: To corrupt a predictable adjacent object on the JVM heap (such as a String or byte[] length header), attackers often send repetitive parameters or headers alongside the malformed Base64 payload to shape memory layout before triggering the out-of-bounds write.
  • Second-Stage Payloads: Once heap corruption gives the attacker control over execution flow or object references, the exploit still needs commands, scripts, or Java gadgets to run. If an exploit chain pairs the initial heap-corruption trigger with a second-stage payload such as shell execution primitives (/bin/sh -c, cmd.exe, reverse-shell strings) or Java class-loading gadgets (java.lang.Runtime, ProcessBuilder, serialized object streams) tucked into another header, query parameter, or request body, cf.waf.score.rce can detect and score that secondary payload as malicious.
  • Post-Exploitation Activity: Even if an initial heap-read or corruption request slips past edge filters, subsequent HTTP requests attempting to interact with an in-memory webshell or pass OS commands to the compromised JVM remain directly visible to WAF Attack Score.

Deploy protections and patch

Because sophisticated in-memory exploits can still execute raw shellcode or manipulate bytecode without ever sending plaintext shell commands over HTTP, WAF Attack Score should be used alongside explicit Base64 rules and JVM patching.

You can find more information on how to deploy Managed rules and attack score in our WAF guide, but in a nutshell:

1. Set the CVE-2026-114938 rule in the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Pro plan and above) to Block. It is enabled in Log mode by default, so review its matches in Security Events first. Use the links on the Cloudflare Zero Wire page to review your rules status.

2. Layer Attack Score to get ML-based remote code execution (RCE) detection: create a custom rule blocking or challenging requests with a low RCE attack score (for example, cf.waf.score.rce le 20 on Enterprise plans, or cf.waf.score.class eq "attack" on Business plans) to catch multi-stage exploit chains and post-exploitation command traffic.

3. Remediate at runtime: Upgrade to patched OpenJDK builds (or set -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as a temporary workaround) to eliminate the vulnerable AVX-512 code path entirely. Follow the OpenJDK advisory and Oracle's Critical Patch Update and install your Java vendor's fixed release as soon as possible. For a prompt you can give an AI agent to inventory your Java runtimes, see the Java4Shell page on Cloudflare Zero Wire. 

Impact on Cloudflare infrastructure

Cloudflare also runs Java, so when Java4Shell was disclosed we checked our own systems. The vulnerability can only be triggered in specific hardware configurations, namely a x86-64 processor that supports AVX-512 VBMI, so a system is exposed only when both are true. Our investigation found that the majority of our Java workloads are not scheduled on vulnerable systems; we took immediate action to protect the remainder.

About an hour after the patches were published, we began rolling out a JVM startup option that turns off the accelerated Base64 routine containing the bug on all Java workloads, so decoding falls back to the standard implementation. To be safe, we are rolling out our patched configuration to all machines, regardless of hardware as a precaution. We have seen no indication so far that Java4Shell was exploited on Cloudflare infrastructure.

Update every Java runtime now

Java4Shell turns a performance optimization in the Java runtime into a path to remote code execution, and with technical details now public, we expect exploit attempts to follow quickly. The fix is to update every Java runtime and restart the services that use it. While you patch, review the new managed rule's matches and switch it to Block if you are on a paid plan and use attack score to catch remote code execution payloads that signatures may miss. 

Our WAF analysts will continue to update protections as new techniques emerge. Follow the WAF changelog for rule updates and the Java4Shell page on Cloudflare Zero Wire for the latest on this vulnerability.

item.title: Quad9’s withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine
item.description: Quad9's forced withdrawal from France highlights the dangers of mandating DNS-level blocking. We explore why forcing public resolvers to act as content filters is technically flawed and threatens the open Internet.
item.dc:creator: Patrick Nemeroff
Christiaan Smits
item.content:encoded:
Last month, the Swiss non-profit foundation Quad9 announced that it will withdraw its free public DNS resolver from France. This difficult decision followed months of litigation and a French court ruling that imposed daily financial penalties on Quad9 for failing to block domains associated with alleged copyright infringement.

Quad9’s departure from France is both disheartening and understandable. The court’s ruling put the organization in the impossible bind of having to choose between crippling litigation and penalties, or fundamentally altering its service in a way that would undermine the privacy and security of its users. Left with no good option, Quad9 is choosing the exit door instead.

The withdrawal of a basic infrastructure service from France fundamentally harms the free and open Internet, and it should serve as a warning of the damage that will result if rightsholders and policymakers continue demanding maximal blocking across every layer of the Internet. It not only deprives French Internet users of a trustworthy and important tool; it creates a real risk of disruption to their daily lives. Quad9’s resolver is used by a wide variety of individuals and organizations in France — including government bodies, educational institutions, hospitals, and utilities — and Quad9 has no way to directly notify those individuals and institutions that their resolver will soon stop working. If the affected parties do not change their resolver before Quad9 removes its service, their Internet will fail with no explanation.

Quad9 is not the first public DNS resolver to withdraw from a country following blocking orders, and it almost certainly won’t be the last. Cisco previously withdrew its OpenDNS resolver from France, Portugal, and Belgium (temporarily) under similar circumstances. And a Belgian court recently issued an order that would impose substantial penalties if Cloudflare, Google, and Cisco do not begin blocking websites through their public resolvers by early January 2027. That’s something Cloudflare has never done.

Cloudflare has spent years advocating against orders of this kind. We are concerned that rightsholders’ unrelenting demands for blocking by public DNS resolvers will end up causing real harm to the Internet.

A refresher on DNS, the Domain Name System

To understand why this is such a problem, it helps to understand how the Internet works under the hood. DNS resolvers are a foundational piece of the Internet’s infrastructure. DNS is the Internet’s address book: when you type a website name such as cloudflare.com, the DNS system translates that domain name into the IP address your device needs to connect to it. A DNS resolver is the service that looks up that address and sends it back to your device, much like an operator finding a phone number in a directory.

DNS resolvers can be operated by anyone, but they are commonly run by Internet service providers (ISPs), mobile networks, businesses, and universities. If you’re reading this blog post at home and have never thought about DNS before, chances are that you’re using your ISP’s default resolver. Because you use your DNS resolver every time that you visit a website, it’s important for it to be reliable and trustworthy.

And because the DNS resolver has access to all of your browsing activity, which resolver you use has real privacy implications.

In addition to DNS resolvers that are provided by your local ISP, there are a variety of public DNS resolvers available. Cloudflare launched our public DNS resolver 1.1.1.1 in April 2018 to give back to the Internet. Our goal was to make a fast, reliable, privacy-first consumer DNS service available for free to everyone. We succeeded. 1.1.1.1 is among the fastest DNS resolvers in the world, including in Europe. Cloudflare's resolver doesn’t collect any user data, let alone sell it to advertisers. 1.1.1.1 has always been one of our favorite examples of Cloudflare fulfilling its mission to help build a better Internet.

1.1.1.1 is one of many public resolvers that anyone can use. In addition to 1.1.1.1 and Quad9’s 9.9.9.9, some of the other best-known public resolvers include Google’s 8.8.8.8 and Cisco’s OpenDNS. Just because these services are offered for free doesn’t mean they’re easy to provide. A well-run global public DNS resolver is an extraordinary engineering feat, built to securely and privately resolve hundreds of billions or even trillions of queries a day across a globally distributed network of hundreds of server locations.

As Quad9 notes, there are many other DNS resolvers available to users, many of them offered by essentially anonymous services whose practices are unknown or undocumented. It’s easy to change your DNS resolver, and people do so for a variety of reasons including performance, reliability, or to access specific security features.

Why public DNS resolvers should not be required to block

Rightsholders have a legitimate interest in preventing online piracy. But trying to address online infringement through public DNS resolvers is fundamentally the wrong approach.

Among other things, such blocking is ineffective. Think back to the analogy of an operator finding a phone number in a directory. If a court wants to shut down an illegal business, forcing the directory operator to cross the business's name out of the phone book doesn't actually close the business. The storefront is still open, the products are still there, and anyone who already knows the address, or uses a different phone book, can walk in.

The same is true for the Internet. DNS resolvers are just one link in the transmission chain. The only way a DNS resolver can “block” content is by declining to return the IP address for a particular website. But a public DNS resolver cannot remove the actual infringing content from the Internet, nor can it take down the servers hosting it.

Because of this, blocking by public DNS resolvers is remarkably easy to bypass. Any Internet user who wants to reach a blocked site can circumvent the block in less than a minute simply by switching to one of the thousands of other DNS resolvers available online. In fact, users don’t even need a resolver at all to reach infringing content if they already know the underlying IP address. Unsurprisingly, while blocking via public resolvers may inject some friction for some users when accessing content, there is no evidence that it actually reduces the total amount of online infringement that occurs.

In addition to being ineffective, as we’ve written previously, DNS blocking is a blunt instrument that causes collateral damage. Because DNS operates at the domain level, a resolver cannot block a specific infringing video or file; it must block the entire domain. This affects all content on that domain, whether legal or illegal. It is also entirely opaque to the user: when a resolver is forced to block a domain, the website simply fails to load. The user receives no explanation or legal notice, making it impossible to know if the site is down for maintenance, if their network is broken, or if the site was blocked by a court order.

The problem is substantially worse with respect to public DNS resolvers. Because public resolvers operate globally, any blocking will naturally cross borders, meaning that a single country could dictate what content is accessible around the world. For example, while the EU-dedicated DNS resolver DNS4EU operated by Whalebone blocks in response to country-specific orders, it does so across the entire EU. Efforts to reengineer public DNS resolvers to allow for more localized blocking would fundamentally alter the service, harming performance and resilience, undermining user privacy, and fragmenting the open Internet.

For these reasons, Cloudflare, Google, Cisco, and Quad9 have all opposed efforts to mandate blocking by public DNS resolvers, with some success. Several years ago, courts in Germany ruled in favor of Cloudflare and Quad9, rejecting requests to require DNS blocking. More recently, a French court rejected penalties against Cloudflare for failing to block through 1.1.1.1, finding that other actions we had taken through our CDN and reverse-proxy service were sufficient to comply with the underlying order.

Undeterred, rightsholders have continued to press for blocking by public resolvers with a level of determination that is hard to explain. A recent study found that the majority of online piracy in Europe is hosted in Europe. If rightsholders want to genuinely address online infringement, there are far better places to focus their efforts — most notably by requiring the hosting providers who actually store the pirated files to take them down.

Forcing public DNS resolvers out of markets hurts the Internet

The French court’s penalty order against Quad9 represents the culmination of these rightsholder efforts. As a small non-profit that only offers a public DNS resolver, Quad9 had no alternative methods for demonstrating compliance with the order. The French court therefore granted rightsholders’ request to issue penalties for non-compliance, forcing Quad9 to undermine its own service or leave the country.

Quad9’s withdrawal from France represents a genuine loss for the Internet. In the short term, removal of Quad9’s resolver is likely to cause immediate and potentially severe disruptions to Internet access. Because of the way their service is set up to preserve privacy, Quad9 has no way to know who exactly is using its resolver, let alone to directly communicate to them about the upcoming withdrawal of services. That means that individuals, hospitals, universities, and government offices all may be caught unaware when the resolver stops working. Again, because of how DNS resolvers work, those users will not receive a detailed error message explaining what happened — their Internet will simply stop working. The problem will be even worse when devices like security systems or thermostats are hardwired to use Quad9’s resolver. Fixing these issues may be slow or even impossible.

More generally, driving Quad9 out of France does absolutely nothing to prevent online infringement, but it does leave everyday Internet users with fewer safe, reliable options, particularly ones like Quad9 that also protect users from phishing and malware. Taking established public DNS resolvers away forces Internet users to fall back on the default resolvers offered by their ISPs (which may monetize their browsing data), try lesser-known resolvers operated by anonymous or less trustworthy organizations, or run their own resolver. The irony is that Quad9 and Cloudflare are being pulled into court precisely because we are transparent, reputable organizations. Penalizing transparent services only pushes users toward less accountable corners of the web.

The way forward

If nothing else, we hope that Quad9’s announcement may serve as a wake-up call to rightsholders and policymakers that seeking to block infringement at every layer of the Internet has real costs.

We believe there are far better ways to work together to fight piracy without compromising the integrity of the Internet, and Cloudflare continues to pursue innovative collaborations to that end. Our collective efforts in addressing online infringement would be put to better use in seeking to have such content removed at the hosting provider, which would both achieve a more durable solution and avoid collateral damage to the Internet.

In the meantime, we will keep resisting misguided efforts to require blocking by public DNS resolvers. Along with Google and Cisco, we have appealed the Belgian order that would impose penalties on us if we do not start DNS blocking by January 2027. We hope to get a resolution before the end of the year that would avoid another situation like the one Quad9 faces now in France.

We have grave concerns about the disruption that would be caused if additional resolvers are forced to withdraw from markets, and we will continue to advocate against that possible result.

item.title: Kitesurf is now open source
item.description: Kitesurf, our experimental browser engine for AI agents, is now open source. Inspect the code, run it locally, or deploy your own instance on Cloudflare Workers.
item.dc:creator: Celso Martinho
Rui Figueira
Bernardo Pereira
Luís Duarte
item.content:encoded:
We introduced Kitesurf, our stateless browser for AI agents that runs entirely on top of Workers, in August and followed up in September with WebMCP support, new APIs, and improved compatibility. On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to.

That promise is now real. Kitesurf is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers.

A browser built for agents

Kitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without a browser container. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can connect clients such as Puppeteer.

Our main goal is to give AI agents a lightweight, efficient browser — one that can load websites, execute JavaScript, and interact with pages while using less CPU and memory than a full browser like Chromium, and scaling on demand across Cloudflare’s global Workers network.

Read more about why and how we built Kitesurf in our initial announcement and how to use it in Browser Run’s developer documentation.

What is inside the repository?

Kitesurf builds on Cloudflare’s Developer Platform and APIs, alongside an ecosystem of open-source Rust packages compiled to WebAssembly:

  • Blitz provides HTML parsing, the DOM, layout, and painting.
  • Stylo provides CSS parsing, cascading, and computed styles.
  • Boa runs JavaScript inside WebAssembly (as the last resort only when we can’t run JavaScript in Dynamic Workers).
  • Linebender libraries provide text layout and 2D graphics, and Krilla generates PDF output.

These projects made Kitesurf possible. They retain their respective licenses; the repository's NOTICE documents third-party notices.

Kitesurf has three main parts: the Engine manages browser sessions and client connections, PageScript runs the page and its JavaScript, and PageRenderer draws the result.

All packages, the engine, its Rust core, DOM shims, renderer, and Kitesurf CLI live separately in folders under the repository’s packages directory where you can explore how all the pieces fit together.

Run your own Kitesurf

To run Kitesurf locally, follow the repository's build requirements, then clone the repository, install dependencies, and start the engine:

git clone https://github.com/cloudflare/kitesurf.git
cd kitesurf
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm run dev

The first build compiles the Rust core and its dependencies, so give it some time. Subsequent builds reuse the build cache. Finally wrangler starts a local development server at http://127.0.0.1:8787. Open that address to try a page in Chrome DevTools, or use it programmatically.

You can use puppeteer with a NodeJS script:

import puppeteer from "puppeteer-core";

const browser = await puppeteer.connect({
  browserWSEndpoint: "ws://127.0.0.1:8787/devtools/browser",
});

try {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  await page.goto("https://example.com/");
  await page.screenshot({ path: "page.png" });
} finally {
  await browser.disconnect();
}

Or you can point your AI harness at the local CDP port (agents love CDP) and watch it take full control of Kitesurf.

Deploy to your Cloudflare account

When you’re done changing and testing locally, you can deploy the engine to your own account and use Kitesurf from there instead of the Browser Run managed APIs we provide. Note that a Workers Paid plan is required because Kitesurf uses Dynamic Workers to create isolated Workers for pages.

From the repository root:

pnpm run deploy

Help us make it better

As with all of our open-sourced projects, Kitesurf lives in Github and we welcome forks and contributions. However, note that Kitesurf is under heavy development and we are focusing on making the engine more compatible (check out Web Platform Test evolution), more reliable, and efficient.

Start with the contribution guidelines if you want to contribute. Open an issue with a minimal reproduction or a proposed approach, and get vouched by a maintainer before opening a pull request. Focused fixes with tests, clear evidence, and a well-defined scope are much easier to review than large rewrites or unrelated cleanup, but all contribution does not have to be code: a small page that reproduces a rendering bug, a failing automation workflow, or a clear documentation correction can help us move forward.

Stay tuned

Kitesurf is evolving quickly. Stay tuned for updates in the blog and our changelog, and keep an eye on the official landing page for the latest on standards compatibility in Web Platform Tests page and benchmarks.

And come chat with the team on Discord. We’re building a browser for agents, and we’d love your help making it better.

item.title: Adapting to AI penetration testing orchestrators: The Modern Security Model
item.description: AI-orchestrated penetration testing platforms like ARTEX have become increasingly powerful tools enabling effective attacks on exposed infrastructure. Here we share Cloudflare’s observations and recommended countermeasures.
item.dc:creator: Blake Darché
Myles Sloan
Jacob Crisp
Cloudforce One
item.content:encoded:
Over the last month, the number of Large Language Model (LLM) penetration testing and orchestration frameworks has exploded. Just a few weeks ago, ARTEX — an open source agentic penetration testing system that automates offensive security workflows — was the only framework available. In just the last three days, we have seen over 50 framework families attempt to scan Cloudflare customers globally. The number of Internet Protocol (IP) addresses seen running these frameworks has grown into the thousands and continues to increase daily. The proliferation of these frameworks has significantly changed the status quo in cyber defense: defenders are struggling to keep up with the volumetric nature of these autonomously guided attacks.

ARTEX was taken down by its creator Autumn-27 on October 8. (“The malicious exploitation of this tool runs entirely counter to its original intent,” they wrote in Chinese.) But in the month since, the ecosystem has exploded with new fragmented versions of it. There are now over 12,000 repositories, with several hundred unique forks containing lineage from the original repository. Additionally, hundreds of other similar agentic orchestration frameworks have been created since October 8. Daily requests of AI penetration testing (pentesting) and exploitation tools has grown by 30x since October 1. These tools have also begun chaining stolen customer credentials in some of the more complex attacks, such as lateral movement chaining throughout an environment.

We expect these frameworks to continue to proliferate, and every organization should be prepared to address this threat. To counter LLM-based pentest frameworks, we recommend that all organizations adopt what we call the Modern Security Model, which has six key pillars:

  • Fortify the front gate: Implement a Web Application Firewall (WAF) with advanced rules such as rate limits.
  • Security station in the foyer: Anomaly detection on all web applications your customers access.
  • Identify phony visitors: Implement Bot Defense.
  • Remove the back door: Implement Identity-Gated Access for all high-risk external and internal web applications.
  • Inspect deliveries: Enforce validated schemas and explicit security controls.
  • Neighborhood watch: Implement Threat Intelligence to gain visibility into attacks.

What is an LLM penetration and exploitation orchestrator?

Open-source pentesting frameworks are able to orchestrate AI agents to carry out stages of the traditional Cyber Kill Chain at scale. Tools like ARTEX have the ability to quickly plug in existing Model Context Protocol (MCP) and connect traditional standalone pentesting tools in novel ways. Some even allow operator direction on what type of task to accomplish. These tools can map and enumerate environments, both from the inside and outside. ARTEX and its forks map assets and environments onto a graph, allowing multiple independent parallel agents to enumerate, verify, prototype, and attack at the speed of inference. These tools turn compromises into a hill-climbable problem, which agents are specifically good at.

The AI LLM pentesting tools that currently exist

We are currently tracking 50+ AI LLM agents. The table below shows the top five LLM penetration and exploitation orchestrators. Each is extremely popular (1k+ GitHub stars) and fully autonomous. The fully autonomous nature of these agents represents a doctrinal shift in offensive cyber capabilities:

  • Human skills are no longer the limit: A harness performs every step of the OODA loop by observing the environment, orienting itself to prioritize valuable and/or vulnerable targets, decide on an action, and act autonomously.
  • Speed increase: Having multiple parallel agents working towards a goal is a large shift compared to single operator or multiple operator augmented by AI.
  • Scale: A single operator can target multiple organizations at the same time, greatly increasing their blast radius.
  • Small mistakes are easily discovered: Autonomous frameworks relentlessly and systematically test exposed services, including their configurations.

Architecture

Post-exploitation capabilities

ARTEX (and forks)

Nothing built-in, requires user instruction

LuaN1aoAgent

Supervisor agent, planner agent, and generic executor agents

Three graphs, with goals/tasks/blockers, evidence/hypothesises/exploits, and target/local

Built-in SSH and Chisel for tunneling and attempted reconnection after disruption

Decepticon

Orchestrator agent dispatching specialist sub-agents

Cairn

Dispatcher orchestrating work to existing AI harnesses (Codex, Claude Code, Pi)

Prompt guidance and Kali tools

PentestGPT-Agent

Supervisor agent and one generic executor agent
